title: Teaching My Father to Distrust His Feed
script: Father: [thoughtful] I don't need a tutorial, Yasmin. I've read that article three times, and it's clearly well-researched.
Yasmin: Can I ask what made it feel well-researched to you, specifically?
Father: [carefully] It cited numbers, it sounded confident, and frankly it confirmed what I already suspected was true.
Yasmin: That last part concerns me more than the first two, honestly. Confirming a prior suspicion is a reason to read something more skeptically, not less.
Father: [reflective] You're suggesting I only believe things that flatter my existing opinions. That's rather insulting, coming from my own daughter.
Yasmin: I'm suggesting all of us do that, myself included, and the feed knows it better than we do, which is precisely why it keeps surfacing exactly this kind of article for you.
Father: [honestly] So the algorithm is choosing my beliefs now? That sounds like the conspiracy theory, not the article.
Yasmin: Not choosing them from nothing, no, but amplifying whichever ones already generate your attention, and attention is the entire currency it's optimizing for.
Father: [gently] Alright, hypothetically, humor me. How would I even tell a well-researched article from a convincing one?
Yasmin: Start by checking whether the same claim, in roughly the same words, appears anywhere outside sources that already agree with each other.
Yasmin: Then it's probably one voice amplified into an echo, which sounds like a chorus but is really just a single opinion bouncing off itself.
Father: [encouraging] I suppose I have occasionally mistaken volume for consensus.
Yasmin: We all have, Dad. I'm not trying to make you paranoid, just slightly slower to nod along before checking.
Father: [seriously] Slower to nod along. At my age, that's practically a personality transplant.
Yasmin: I'll settle for a slight renovation. The transplant can wait for next year.

quiz.question: Why did the father initially find the article well-researched?
options: It cited numbers, sounded confident, and confirmed what he already suspected
A friend recommended it
It was published by a university
It had many positive comments
quiz.explanation: The father says it cited numbers, sounded confident, and confirmed his existing suspicions.

quiz.question: Why does Yasmin say confirming a prior suspicion should prompt more skepticism?
options: It shouldn't matter at all
Because it's a reason to read something more skeptically, not less, since we all favor flattering opinions
Because confirmed suspicions are always false
Because it means the source is paid
quiz.explanation: Yasmin explains that confirming a prior suspicion is a reason for more skepticism, not less, since everyone favors flattering information.

quiz.question: What does Yasmin say the algorithm optimizes for?
options: Factual accuracy
Random selection of content
Attention, amplifying whichever beliefs already generate engagement
Educational value
quiz.explanation: Yasmin says attention is the entire currency the algorithm optimizes for, amplifying beliefs that generate it.

quiz.question: What test does Yasmin suggest for checking a claim?
options: Checking the number of likes it received
Asking a friend for their opinion
Checking only the publication date
Checking whether the same claim appears outside sources that already agree with each other
quiz.explanation: Yasmin suggests checking whether the claim appears outside sources that already agree with each other.

quiz.question: What does the father admit by the end of the conversation?
options: That he has occasionally mistaken volume for consensus
That the article was completely false
That he will stop using the internet
That Yasmin is wrong about everything
quiz.explanation: The father admits he has occasionally mistaken volume for consensus.

quiz.question: What central claim does “Teaching My Father to Distrust His Feed” develop?
options: Convenience can quietly replace forms of deliberate connection.
Critical media literacy requires questioning a feed’s incentives.
Personalisation can infer patterns without genuine understanding.
Being reachable should remain a choice, not an obligation.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects limits of automated claims and accountable technology use.

options: The landline’s limits shape a different kind of availability.
The algorithm’s prediction exposes how much data is collected.
The father’s feed rewards repetition and emotional certainty.
Constant availability blurs work and private boundaries.

options: Nostalgia does not prove older tools were universally better.

Connectivity does not require surrendering all privacy.
Popularity does not establish accuracy or fairness.
